result:
There is a strange, persistent illusion that time speeds up the older we get. When we are children, a single summer stretches out like an endless continent of sunlit afternoons, scraped knees, and the slow-motion agony of waiting for a birthday. December to December is an epoch. But somewhere along the way, the gears of the clock seem to catch fire. Years begin to blur into months, and months into weeks, until you wake up wondering how a decade slipped through your fingers while you were busy answering emails and folding laundry. 

Perhaps the reason for this acceleration is that childhood is defined by *firsts*. Every experience is pristine, unmapped territory. Your brain is working overtime to record the world because everything is novel. You remember the exact texture of the bark on that specific tree you climbed when you were seven because it mattered; it was a sensory onslaught. But adulthood, by necessity, becomes an exercise in efficiency. We build routines to save cognitive energy. We commute the same way, drink the same coffee, and navigate the same social structures. The brain, wonderfully adaptive, stops paying close attention to the mundane details. And when you stop recording the details, time stops leaving footprints. The days dissolve into a nameless, faceless continuum.

This realization is both terrifying and liberating. It’s terrifying because it highlights the sheer velocity of mortality. But it’s liberating because it offers a prescription: if you want to slow time down, you have to break the routine. You have to force your brain to wake up. 

Travel is the most obvious antidote. When you touch down in a city where you don't speak the language, where the street signs are cryptic hieroglyphs and the smell of the air is entirely foreign, time undergoes a radical dilation. A three-day trip can feel like a lifetime because every single moment requires active engagement. You can’t autopilot when you’re trying to figure out the subway system in Tokyo or navigating a labyrinthine alleyway in Marrakech. 

Yet, we can’t all be perpetual globetrotters. Most of our lives are lived in the margins—in the Tuesday afternoons, the grocery store aisles, and the quiet hours before sleep. The real challenge, the real art of living, is finding a way to inject novelty and mindfulness into the ordinary. What if we looked at our hometowns with the wide-eyed curiosity of a tourist? What if we actually tasted our food instead of inhaling it while scrolling through a glowing rectangle of bad news? What if we listened to people—really listened—without immediately drafting our rebuttal in our heads?

Speaking of glowing rectangles, we are living through an unprecedented psychological experiment. Never before in human history has humanity carried around a device that connects them to the sum total of human knowledge, while simultaneously functioning as a slot machine designed to hijack our dopamine receptors. We are perpetually tethered to the collective anxiety of eight billion people. If there is a famine in a country you’ve never heard of, a stock market fluctuation halfway across the globe, or a minor celebrity saying something foolish, you know about it instantly. 

Our nervous systems were simply not built for this. We evolved to care about the tribe of fifty people immediately surrounding us, the weather patterns in our immediate valley, and the immediate threat of a predator in the bushes. When we flood our ancient brains with a 24-hour firehose of global crisis, we live in a state of chronic, low-grade panic. We feel guilty for sitting still because we feel like we should be *doing* something, *reading* something, *optimizing* something.

This is why boredom has become a endangered species, and it is a tragedy. Boredom is the fertile soil of the imagination. Some of the greatest breakthroughs in art, science, and philosophy happened not when people were frantically searching for answers, but when they were staring out of windows, letting their minds wander into the wilderness. When we kill every moment of silence with a podcast, a scroll, or a video, we suffocate the inner voice that has the most interesting things to say to us.

We need to reclaim the lost art of doing nothing. Not "self-care" as marketed by wellness brands—which usually just means buying another expensive product to add to your shelf—but genuine, unstructured, unproductive nothingness. Sit on a porch and watch the wind move through the grass. Stare at a wall. Lie on the rug and listen to an entire album from start to finish without looking at a screen. It feels uncomfortable at first, almost like an itch you aren't allowed to scratch. But on the other side of that discomfort is a profound sense of decompression. 

It makes you realize how much of our lives are spent performing. We perform competence at work, we perform happiness on social media, we perform politeness in social settings. We wear social armor because the world can be a harsh and judgmental place. But taking off the armor—even if only for an hour, even if only in the privacy of your own mind—is essential for spiritual survival.

There is a wonderful poem by Mary Oliver where she asks, *“Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?”* It’s a heavy question, often quoted on graduation cards and inspirational posters, but its familiarity shouldn't dull its edge. Because the truth is staggering in its simplicity: this is it. There is no dress rehearsal. The person you were ten years ago is gone, the person you will be in ten years is a stranger, and right now, in this exact, fleeting second, you are experiencing the absolute peak of your existence. 

We spend so much time preparing to live. We suffer through jobs we hate to buy things we don't need to impress people we don't like, all under the delusion that the real life will start *after* the next promotion, *after* the move, *after* we finally get our act together. But life isn't waiting for you in the future. It’s happening right here, in the creak of the floorboards, the hum of the refrigerator, the dull ache in your lower back, the complex flavor of a cup of coffee.

If you can manage to wake up to that fact—even for a few minutes a day—the illusion of fast-moving time begins to fracture. The days stop slipping through your fingers like sand. Instead, they become heavy, golden, and real. You start to collect moments rather than just passing through them. 

So, what should we do with this freedom? Perhaps we should be a little kinder to ourselves and to one another. We are all, after all, just improvising our way through a cosmic mystery, navigating the dark with no map, trying to figure out how to be human. We are terrified of getting it wrong, of being forgotten, of not measuring up. But beneath all that fear is a staggering capacity for joy, for connection, for awe. 

Look up from the screen. Notice the way the light hits the wall right now. Breathe in deeply, hold it for a second, and let it go. You are alive. That is the only miracle that matters.
